review: Great game, BUT...I can't see slimes because I am red-green colorblind. Please add a colorblind mode.

The actual gameplay is really fun. The only thing is that the controls are the worst thing to every exist. I had to spend 20 minutes just fixing all the controls because they were that messed up and confusing.

It's sad to give this a "not recommended", because there's a lot to like in Moonlighter.  It's not really a "bad" game, but there's not a lot of depth to it, and it has a huge number of small annoyances that end up making the game feel incredibly clumsy to play.

The shop mechanics are... fine, but you basically do the same thing with every type of item.  Figure out the best price for the item (you do this by semi-randomly trying out different prices unitl the customers show a certain face), then put all the shit you don't think you need up for sale at that best price.  You sit in your shop and wait for customers to come in, bring an item to you, then you hit A.  Occasionally a shopliflter will come in and you have to run and stop them, after which the item falls on the ground and you have to re-put it up for sale.  There's just not a lot going on in this section of the game.

So is the combat worth it?  Well... kinda.  It's, again, fine, but nothing special.  You have a few different types of weapons (which can be upgraded in town).  There's an alternative attack (which is usually a super underpowered charge attack), and a normal attack.  You can also dodge-roll.  The enemies look nice and aren't terrible to fight, but something feels just a bit too slow and awkward about the fighting.

You also have to do constant inventory management during your dungeon runs.  There are 3 floors to each dungeon, but you'll probably be full after 75% of the first floor.  This means that after every room, you're often opening your inventory, trying to figure out which stuff to dump (you can convert all objects to money while in the dungeon), and then going to the next room.  This really breaks up any attempts at "flow", and the sheer NUMBER of different items is really silly.  They tried to mix things up with an "item curse" system, where some items have to be placed in specific spots, or other items destroy items in certain adjacent slots if you return to town, but this system doesn't really work at all, it just makes the whole process more annoying (you can't stack "normal" items with cursed variants).

And the small nitpicks... there are so many small things that get in the way of enjoying the game.

- Want to craft healing potions?  Select the potion, hit A on the potion, move the cursor from "no" to "yes", hit A again, wait for a short animation.  Now repeat if you wanted more than 1 potion (which you always do).
- Upgrading your shop or adding a merchant?  Get locked in an awkward animation where a random builder guy SLOWLY walks from off screen to where the shop will be, the screen fades out, then again the builder SLOWLY walks back off screen.
- Have an item held in your cursor and try to swap it out with another item?  The item doesn't come into your cursor, it goes to where the original item was, so now you have to move back to that item to move it again.
- No way to quick-sell items in the inventory
- No mouse support at all, so you can't really speed up inventory management
- Buying items doesn't remove them from your "wishlist", so you have to do that manually
- Upgrading/decorating your shop seems interesting at first, but the impact it has feels very minimal
- The dungoen design is really repetitive, and no rooms really feel unique in any way.  
- "harder" enemy variants are the exact same but just do more damage and have more health
- Many enemies can be cheesed extremely easily by hitting them through the solid level pieces with your weapon
- "Story" text that you find in the dungeons repeats itself, and you can't skip them once you've started reading them (and there are a few that are 10+ dialog boxes worth of text).
- Each "run" feels extremely similar, as you don't get any mid-run upgrades

I could go on for more.  The art is great, the sound/music is fine, but man the game is lacking in actual fun design.

Games like this make me hate steams review system.  The game is fun, but it's pretty lacklustre to be honest.  Only 5 bosses, randomly generated maps, paper-thin story line, barely engaging shop system, and the most straight forward weapons and armor you've ever seen.  

Have you seen the trailer? Well, you've pretty much seen everything worth seeing as far as story is concerned.  The rest is basically an old man who tells you to stay outta the dungeons constantly, well the ending is weird. There are various notes hinting at a deeper storyline, but they're kinda disjointed and uninteresting.  Mainly because what they actually reveal in the end is kinda stupid.  

The monsters are pretty good, solid enemies.  Lot's of creative patterns. The bosses are also consistent and solid challenges.  The main problem is that you can pretty much just buy your way through any dungeons you're having trouble with.  As the game goes on, your income becomes stupidly high and every time you return from a dungeon without dieing, you can make a massive profit.  Then you can just upgrade or enchant your weapons, load your inventory up with potions and then the whole dungeon is basically free.  

That brings us to the next problem, the over-simplified weapon and armor choices.  They literally boil down to, do you want armor that makes you: 
1)faster with weak defense
2)average speed average defense
3)slower with stronger defense.  
Those are LITERALLY your armor choices.  And your weapons aren't much better.  

Everything about this game is over-simplified.  They figured since they were basically making a game with two different concepts, they could skimp on both.  Whether it's the shopping or the combat, neither one is anywhere near complete.

I'm not usually the kind of guy that writes reviews about games, but I feel that it must be said. 

This is a great game concept. However, the execution needs work. 

Gameplay wise, the way the game flows makes it difficult to continue playing. Going into dungeons and selling artifacts feels more and more like a chore instead of this great thing you're doing for Rynoka.  I do enjoy that during some of the game, you don't necessarily have to watch over Moonlighter. At about a halfway point in the game, you can hire someone to watch over the shop which is a great change of pace. But at the same time, I felt myself not wanting to waste money on someone who might get stolen from, so rarely did I use the assistant.

I did finish this game, just once, and once some of the updates started coming out I was in the mood to play it again. My patience however had died down. The flaws in the game become much more realised in a second playthrough, where you know what you're doing. When you're just selling to customers, you're barely paying attention. The little side quests to go back into the dungeons and retrieve artifacts for certain quests never felt worth it enough to do and I never saw a form of punishment for not doing them after they were accepted.

Everything else is really good. I love this game's soundtrack, art style, controls (which is surprising, because learning them was tough for me at first) and story. While the story really isn't a driving force to keep playing, it is still interesting enough for me to at least wonder what exactly is going on with the dungeons. Even though the ending kind of kills the hype, for me, the mystery behind it is very neat.

So overall, I would say the game is about a 6/10 and I would reccomend this game. However, only to anyone new to this sort of genre of games. On paper. this game sounds extremely fun. The idea of a shopkeep who runs into the dungeons to get materials is such a great idea for a game but again, the execution is done poorly.

I regret being on the fence about buying this game. I've been loving it ever since i picked it up. It has that Stardew valley feel to it, but unfortunately without most of the things that makes that game adorable. On the flip side, it's reminiscient of Legend of Zelda games, and is entirely focused on clearing dungeon floors, sort of like the Binding of Isaac.

I'll try doing a pros / neutral / cons thing for this review, for once.

PROS:
+ Very charming and smooth pixel graphics á la Starbound Valley

+ Gameplay is something like Recettear meets Legend of Zelda with storytelling like Rogue Legacy

+ Relatively fast paced and reaction / pattern intensive. Mildly hardcore but not unfair!

+ Clearly inspired by older Legend of Zelda games, such as those found on GBA

+ Magical soundtrack, parts of it dynamic (changes while playing based on what you are doing or where you are). It's the kind of music you never really get tired of listening to. Very catchy and mix-up intensive.

+ No enemy recycling - every biome has its own unique enemies, and some only show up on lower floors or at night

+ Clever randomized map design with secrets to find, encourages exploring

+ NPC writing is good, if rather lacking in quantity... (Will elaborate)

+ There is no hard time limit. Like Starbound Valley but without seasons or a day clock.

+ Interesting, fair bosses with no "learn by death" patterns. If you pay attention you can overcome everything.

+ The default difficulty is "Hard". That's not something i've ever seen before, but it can be adjusted if you want to.

+ Every armor piece shows on your character, and they can freely be mixed and matched at your leisure. 

+ You decide prices of items you sell. This can be stressful and confusing if you do not like thinking.

+ Dark background world / story that belies the cute graphics. You have to piece this together yourself.

+ Very interesting dungeons with unique aesthetics and suitable music.

Now for the neutrals. I will put these in because they could be a matter of opinion or playstyle - some people won't mind this at all, while for others it can be very disappointing.

NEUTRAL:

\ The game is a rather short one. Few weapon upgrades (although progression locked due to material requirements)

\ Besides grinding for money, there's very little else to do than conquer the dungeon. Once you unlock everything...

\ ..You no longer have anything to do in town except resupply. 

\ Small inventory forcing you to manage it wisely, and return to town often or throw items away.

\ Clever curse system on items that requires different and still clever inventory management.

\ I doubt there's anything to do after conquering the few dungeons. They are fun, but... Mobile game-length.

\ NPCs do not remember conversations. They will repeat themselves endlessly.

\ Random town NPCs share lines. If you talk to multiple in a row they will finish each other's monologues.

\ Some NPCs have portraits when they talk, yet no more significance than any other NPC. Scrapped story assets?

\ There is no player-NPC interaction. They will only ever monologue to you. No decisions or similar.

\ Good shop management is not actually important as you can endlessly grind for items in the dungeons.

\ As you have a monopoly on the market, there is no flooding the economy. Endless money!

\ No real attack variation. Usually not a problem but lacks the flair of better hack&slash games when it comes to combat.

\ You cannot hire guards to your store or expel repeat offenders. Thieves will constantly leave and come back immediately.

\ You also have to wait for said thieves to commit a crime before you can stop them, even if you know them well already.

\ Movement in six directions, for the most part. Walking diagonally feels unresponsive, but it's there.

\ You only attack in four directions. This is alright as so do your enemies. Easily exploitable with our flexibility.

\ Your character is (barely) established - no backstory, but everybody in town knows you.

CONS:

- Each weapon class has ONE special attack, regardless of what weapon type or tier you have. This attack SUCKS.

- The town feels very bare-bones. As if there was more planned for it, but then it was all scrapped once they had the shell.

- The other NPCs than your guide / tutor never gets fleshed out. They seem designed to have a larger part in the story.

- While the other NPCs have good writing in itself (elaborating on their stories and their society as a whole) they do not

- Play any significant part in the game and you can easily ignore them without missing out on anything.

- The only real reason to even manage the shop is to afford adventuring upgrades. Cynical and repetitive.

- Eventually guessing prices for new items can get overwhelming as there are a lot of items and no price references.

I have probably missed out on a couple things, but overall i still recommend this game. It's a great experience (especially when just starting out) and it's an enjoyable dungeon crawler / loot collecting game with generally satisfying gameplay.

Please ask questions in the comments field if there is anything specific you would like to know, or for me to add to the review.

Moonlighter looks and sounds fantastic—the pixel art, soundtrack, and shopkeeper-meets-dungeoneer premise are genuinely charming.

Unfortunately, the novelty wears off fast. The gameplay loop quickly turns into a monotonous grind of looting, selling, and upgrading with little variety. The combat feels frustratingly stiff, hampered by clunky dodge rolls and awkward hitboxes. Worst of all, the shop management is surprisingly undercooked, boiling down to mindless trial-and-error pricing rather than any deep strategy.

It has plenty of charm, but the shallow mechanics make it hard to recommend unless it's on a steep discount.

Most of the games that I don't recommend, I say "I wish I could recommend this..." and that's the case with [i]Moonlighter[/i] as well. A lot of people like it, and you might be one of them! But I'm not. 

[i]Moonlighter[/i] introduces a very cool premise as being a shopkeeper who ventures into dungeons to get loot to sell in their store. The dungeons themselves feel reminiscent of the original [i]Legend of Zelda[/i], and the notion of selling things is a nice way to break up the dungeon crawling aspect. (The dungeon interiors being randomized also helps) 

You have the option of investing further in your store, in the town, and being able to upgrade and enchant your equipment. There's a nice, fairly constant, feeling of advancement. You learn what to sell items for, what demand will be like, which dungeons to hit and when to cut your losses. 

Your bags fill up quickly and you have to decide what's worth taking with you and what's worth dropping, and that's interesting. While a lot of games have a good risk / reward system, this one actually succeeds in making that feel like it matters to your character as more than just "oh you're dead now". Failure means not getting paid, failure means your shop not succeeding. Failure could mean losing a quest from someone who is willing to pay a fortune if you could just find 3 more rocks to bring them. 

All of this is great on paper, and don't get me wrong, the art is simply gorgeous, and clearly a ton of work has been put into this. 

But the main problem is that there's no depth or nuance to these activities. Every single floor of the dungeon, sometimes multiple times, you're doing inventory management. Every single time you find a new item, you're doing trial and error to find out what you should price it at. It's always the same, and after a few hours you might (as I did) just sigh and say, "Yeah, I get the idea." wishing that there was something more coming.

I also had problems with the combat, which ranges from being simply bland ("oh, it's just this again"), to annoying ("what goddamn angle is he at that I can't hit him with this swing's arc?"), to frustratingly hurling your own corpse at the boss until you learn the three patterns he uses (what I call the "Dark Souls combat isn't actually interesting" problem).

It's by no means a bad game. It's fine, it's okay, I just wish there was more to it.

I actually really like this game in principle. The adventure game in the dungeons is fun and, at the highest difficulty level, adequately challenging. Even more appealing, for me, is the shop keeping game that your character does during the day. However, unfortunately it is exactly that second aspect that has what is to me a game-breaking bug, although it might seem silly to some, a bug that has been in the game for four years at least, according to discussions here on Steam and on Reddit.

While selling items in your shop, you can experiment with the pricing, and based on the reactions of your customers can work out whether to raise or lower the price for that particular item, depending also on the popularity of that item at the moment. The data you gather with this experimentation are recorded in a shop keeper's notebook, so that eventually you are able to learn the optimal prices for each item.

Or you should be, because it seems that for some items, at some point, the notebook stops working. It's not clear how or why, but the price points associated with certain positive or negative reactions from the customers just do not update anymore in this book. To me, that sort of removes the main selling point of the shop keeping side of the game, which was itself, for me, the main selling point of the game as a whole.

Since this bug bothers me so much, and since it has been reported multiple times since May 2018 at least, and since the developers apparently never reacted to or addressed this bug, I have decided to post a negative review (and to stop playing the game). Sadly, because in truth, the game still does appeal to me. If this bug is ever fixed, I would happily update my review to a positive one—and jump right back in, again.

I debated whether to recommend or not. Overall, I love the concept of the game. I think the idea of running a shop using the loot you gain from raiding dungeons is wonderful. The graphics are fantastic as well. That being said, I think the combat and gameplay could be more enjoyable. I struggled to stay invested for the long term.

7/10

Beside these two, the games lacks a lot. I finished the entire game abusing the second attack of the long sword which gives you invulnerability during its animation.

I gotta say that the story is pretty interesting and it was nice to see glimpses of the history of each "dungeon" through the description of the items.

TL;DR
I don't think this game is worth buying because there are a lot better options out there that provide way more enjoyment. If you really want to try the trading system, wait for sale. 

Do not buy this game at full price!

tl;dr: An extremely well-polished game as far as graphics and sound design go, but lacks any real depth in gameplay. The game has a lot of interesting systems, but none of them have any real bite to them to keep you engaged.

This game draws heavy inspiration from Recettear as far as the basic design, and improves on the combat of Recettear by quite a lot. However, pretty much all depth is taken out of the shop management side of things. There is never any pressure that you will run out of gold, or any hard decisions you have to make surrounding capital management. If you run low on money, you can just go and grind dungeons until you have enough. In fact, the only pressure in the game at all comes from not wanting to waste your time grinding. The shop system itself is pretty one dimensional, where upgrades are all pretty boring stat increases, with nothing really unique like the atmosphere system in Recettear. There are two interesting systems where customers are only willing to wait in line for a certain amount of time, and thieves that will come into your shop and try to steal things. However, again there is no pressure on either of these two systems. I have never had someone get sick of waiting in line and leave, nor has a thief ever managed to steal an item because they are extremely easy to stop. Upgrades for weapons and gear are also equally boring, with everything having flat stat upgrades and special abilities that are lackluster and almost never worth using. Overall the game has a lot of promise, but feels like it’s in early access with half of the core game mechanics missing.

The concept is good in theory but it really lacks depth. The entire game is very mindless and you just grind until you make progress.

Hell, I beat the final boss just by walking up to him, mashing the attack button, and using potions until he died before I did. I literally spared no thought to his attacks and I won on my first try.

Good game idea, addictive gameplay, let down by poor controls, inconsistent hit detection on inbound damage, a multitude of softlocks, and an overall lack of polish in terms of input handling and UI.

Poor controls:
- 8-way movement, but only 4-way facing. Makes positive use of the analog stick tricky -- when you move diagonal is subject to finnicky zones, cutting between up/down or left/right movement alongside diagonal movement. When using the d-pad, diagonal movement always faces the character up or down, never left or right, making targeting a hassle.
- Ledges are finnicky. Sometimes you fall down a pit with practically no provocation, sometimes you have to lean on it for half a second before you actually jump down. Rolling over double-wides in anything but ideal conditions has about even odds of you seeing the other side vs. seeing the door you came in on.
- Incoming damage is extremely unpredictable. Sometimes projectiles will hit hard cover, sometimes they'll burst through it like it's not even there -- what finally set me off that it wasn't me was the fact that standing in the exact same location behind a pillar, two long-wise lava streams passed me... the first one missing completely, the second nailing me.
- The register in the store can be tempermental, sometimes requiring repositioning three or four times before allowing sales to a waiting customer.

Poor UI:
- A keyboard is also cool -- not. While I could get to the menu with the keyboard/gamepad switch option, I was unable to figure out which key to press to actually get the UI to switch to the keyboard controls so I could see the rest of them. Gave up and just plugged in a gamepad.
- No "sort my storage/inventory" option.
- No "repack my storage/inventory" option.
- Walking into the dungeon resets any teleport you might have set -- without warning, and without any ability to get it back. The teleport by your shop is just far enough out of eyeshot that it's quite possible to make it out of town without noticing you have a port up.
- With no fast way to switch cursor between storage and inventory when placing cursed items -- and causing items to be switched between inventories when over-placing directly -- that "mini game" becomes bounds more tedious and much less enjoyable than it otherwise would be.
- No min/max recording in the merchant book regarding price reactions, making finding the highest "ideal" price mildly obnoxious.
- Price reactions frequently fail to be recorded in the merchant book, making finding the highest "ideal" price an active headache.
- Price bubbles on tables' lower items cover up the item above them, making keeping track of what's actually out/on sale an annoyance.
- Trying to cursor in the up-direction to the top-left storage inventory slot causes the UI to switch to the previous chest, instead of selecting the desired topmost-leftmost item
- Not being able to save and put the game down at any time is an annoyance.
- Wishlisted item components show as wishlisted... even when they're supposed to be "unknown."

Silver linings:
- GREAT choice to allow crafting with vendors so long as you own the items needed -- they don't have to be in your inventory.
- GREAT choice to allow wishlisting stuff, so you don't accidentally sell necessary crafting materials.

Road to 100%: Game #14

If I am going by Steam’s metric for game reviews, then no. No, I would not recommend this game to other players. Is Moonlighter a terrible game? Certainly not, although I did want to scream such at the top of my lungs at times. It is clear a significant amount of passion and effort went into this game, seeing as it is the only child of Digital Sun. However, I found this game to be deeply flawed wholistically, and I intend to discuss that in detail. 

I have been waiting to write this review since my second hour of gameplay. Let’s start with the good stuff.

The game is obviously gorgeous. The 8-bit, Legend of Zelda Rougelite has such a charming style and color palette, it’s certainly what made me stop by in the Steam Store. The dungeons look great, the bosses are cool, the town is quaint and cozy. Even the enemies in each dungeon have their own way of looking cute, like you could just pick each one up and put it in your pocket. The animators did a really wonderful job here.
What drew me to this game in particular was the concept. Go out, adventure and loot, and then return to your shop to sell to other adventurers. And for the most part, that mechanic was entertaining; instead of the normal “sell all” found in most looters, it’s a core part of the gameplay that requires your attention. I had fun learning what items were the most valuable in each dungeon and planning accordingly. I also liked the item curse mechanic, it made inventory management more rewarding and engaging.

That’s about it. Let’s get into what I hated about this game, because it’s the only reason I’m excited to write this review.

I need to start with the combat. It’s just abhorrent. Attacking in Moonlighter is so goddamn clunky, regardless of the weapon; having Will come to a full stop when attacking makes combat incredibly slow and cumbersome. The only two viable playstyles were either slow and bow or just dive headfirst with a melee weapon and try to clear the room as fast as possible while tanking damage. This perhaps could have been solved by including more variable weapon types or upgrades, but instead we just had 5 weapons with two attacks each and status effect upgrades. Nothing felt rewarding about the combat. To call it challenging would be giving it too much credit.

Next, I want to talk about hitboxes because they’re also abhorrent. It’s unclear as to whether this is a miscommunication between animators and designers or was intentional game design, but throughout my gameplay I found the hitboxes to be incredibly inconsistent. At times, hitboxes felt pixel perfect, following the exact animation on screen. And other times, they seemed to follow their own set of rules and physics, not related to the animation at all. And this applied to every hitbox: my attacks, enemy attacks, bosses, trees, status effects on the ground, holes in the floor. I swear it was harder to intentionally jump down into a secret room than it was to clear a room in this game.

Remember how I mentioned earlier that I liked the idea of the concept, the shop owner bullshit? Yeah, that mechanic lost its magic after the first hour of gameplay. Not because of the store management and finding the perfect price and organizing, no, I actually really enjoyed that aspect of it. It was the way Moonlighter scales the value of its items and in-game market. It was so deflating to spend all this time defeating the first dungeon and obtaining seemingly high value boss items, only for them to be immediately devalued by basic loot I can find on the second floor of the next dungeon. The same went for weapons and armor, these tools that you’ve worked an arm and a leg for on your first play through go from God-slayers to stick and stones in the blink of an eye. The scaling in this game was just so crazy, it felt like they game was just following a formula as opposed to a well thought out and intentionally designed in-game market. It was only an hour in when I realized that Moonlighter was just one small concept, copy and pasted 4 times. 4 Dungeons, 3 floors each, enemies, damage, health, loot, money, all just scaling at the same rate, always just out of reach. It was then that I realized that this seemingly cool concept was not done justice.
 
A counter-argument to this point above may be, “well, this game is a Roguelite, it is supposed to be repetitive.” I agree with that. But this just ain’t it. Dying doesn’t matter. You just lose items, not the run, not the build. It’s just an inconvenience, not a mechanic. Just because it flows like Binding of Isaac and has random loot and you die sometimes doesn’t excuse this game’s lack of depth.

I will say the achievements in this game were fun to chase, albeit the “perfect” boss achievements and the “Savage!” achievement were extremely frustrating to obtain. To expect such precision in a game that is so imprecise. To expect such commitment to a game that has such low replayability. Have some self-awareness please.
 
DLC was fun.

And now please enjoy this list of other gripes I had about Moonlighter:
-	The Banker is hilariously useless
-	Familiars negating Will’s attacks when doing damage
-	Audio bugs whenever entering a Merchant Emblem portal
-	No button to drop items from inventory 
-	No button to quick-sell items to the Mirror instead of moving item to Mirror
-	Wanderer Items are useless but act like they are somehow OP
-	Still unclear why this game couldn’t have been programmed for mouse and keyboard

Because there's a lot of good about it. Decent music, gorgeous graphics, and an interesting premise.

But unfortunately it tries to do two things at once and ends up being mediocre at both.

The combat side is what you expect from a Roguelite isometric action game. To be fair, it does give a variety of enemies with different moves, so you can't turn your brain off.

However, it still boils down to dodge/block, attack, and repeat.

And since they sometimes throw so much at you that you inevitably take a hit and you gotta take down enemies quickly before the timer gives way to a reaper like enemy, you'll be throwing a lot of money at gear/upgrades. So the game turns into a grindfest unless you want to completely cheese it. And you can only play the dungeons so many times before they grow stale.

Then there's the shop aspect....which Recettear did way better years ago.

Recettear has characters you get to know and interact with, complex sale system, and a monthly debt that puts the pressure on. You could play the game without the dungeon aspect and still enjoy it.

With Moonlighter, none of the NPCs have any kind of distinct personality and the shop doesn't require anything other than guessing and setting the correct price while watching out for obvious shoplifters.

It's fun at first but you soon realize that it's no different than hording and selling your loot in Skyrim but with an extra step.

As I've said, it's not bad. I really wish Steam added a thumb sideways. There's some enjoyment and it might be worth it when it's on sale for a few bucks. But if you looking for a great shop game, get Recettear. If you're looking for a great dungeon crawler, get something like Hyper Light Drifter or Hades. But if you want something that's just ok at both, get this one.

Moonlighter is first and foremost a dungeon crawling game with strong memories of Legend of Zelda. Meanwhile the shop management segment will rarely have you shouting "Capitalism, ho!"

While I wanted desperately to like this game, it just isn't what was advertised. The current marketing implies story progression and characterization, companions/pets, a crafting system, haggling with shoppers, etc.

It's actually a roguelike (sort of), and not a great one. And If it had included any of the above, that would have been enough for me. But instead:

- There isn't any story, other than what's listed in the game description. I'm not sure why our main character was even given a name.

- The NPCs in town are named and have unique sprites, but most share the same generic dialogue. There is no relationship building or personality created for any of them. 

- Dungeons and monsters are more or less the same as you progress, other than stats being doubled with each new tier (and some reskins based on the dungeon theme. Gray enemies in the cave. Green enemies in the forest.) Gameplay in Dungeon #2 is exactly the same as in Dungeon #1, except the numbers are bigger.

- Equipment "crafting" is also a straightforward double-your-stats with each new tier. You have only two choices per weapon; higher damage or a status effect. Again, the low and high tier weapons are used identically — except the numbers are bigger.

- Your "companions" are tiny sprites of in-dungeon enemies. (I say "companions" because that's how it's advertised in the game description.) One of the graphics in the marketing shows a pet following you with a little heart. This is not in the game. There is no "pet" or "befriend" mechanic, you simply unlock them by defeating an enemy a certain number of times.

- The loot discovered in dungeons is themed... but it's all just vendor trash (even if you yourself are the vendor.) The twigs you find in Dungeon #2 are functionally equivalent to the rocks you find in Dungeon #1 — except the numbers are bigger.

In all, if you've played the game for 2 or so hours, you've unknowingly already discovered all there is to discover. Unless you like numbers that get bigger.

Finally — yes, this game does get unfairly compared to Recettear. It isn't Recettear, and it shouldn't have to be Recettear. But if it's marketing itself on its story/companions/crafting/haggling when it doesn't contain those elements, it's hard not to make the comparison.

I wanted to like this game, I'm a huge fan of "run shop and do other thing" games like Recettear, but this game just did not deliver for me. The game's dungeons aren't fun, the shopkeeping isn't interesting, and they don't tie together in ways that I find satisfying.

Let's start with the combat, since the game itself does the same. Crawling through dungeons is moving from enclosed rectangle to enclosed rectangle and fighting every enemy inside before moving on to the next enclosed rectangle. The combat feels clunky, most weapons are slow and you get animation locked for doing anything with them. And as for the weapons themselves, there are 5 different types and each weapon gets a grand total of 2 attacks. You can only attack in 4 directions, and with as many enemies as the game throws at you combined with the slow weapons and animation lock makes combat feel more frustrating than fun as you struggle to align yourself correctly to actually hit enemies without dying. The weapons themselves also offer little variety, the bow and spear function very similarly with "hitting things in a line from reasonably far away" while the sword-and-shield and big sword do the same with "sweep weapon in an arc," with the last weapon being fisticuffs with such an abysmal range you'll struggle to deal damage without taking contact damage first. And as you go through the dungeons, the environments themselves add even more hassle to consider, making the already aggravating combat truly infuriating.

The shopkeeping is very basic. You put items on a shop, list their price, and wait for people to buy it. The only thing that vaguely counts as gameplay here is setting the price, you have to figure out what it's worth yourself, but once you've solved that riddle then it's just putting the items in display cases and calling it a day. The game alludes to a supply and demand system, but I've literally never noticed it affect my gameplay. There can also be thieves show up to try and steal stuff, but it's literally the same character sprite for the thief every single time and he lingers for so long before trying to steal something that it barely counts as a distraction.

As for how the shop and dungeon interact, you'd barely notice the difference between this game and a more straightforward roguelite. The only difference is that instead of picking up money, you pick up items to sell, and I've already talked about the shopkeeping. The inventory management itself does actually have potential, items have a bunch of curses that affect where specifically in your bag you can put stuff, and you sometimes have to choose if you want to keep an expensive item to sell or a stack of materials for upgrades. But again, the shop itself does so little here, and you'd make those same choices if you didn't have to open a shop to sell items yourself.

So, besides the shop and dungeons, what's here? Nothing. The story is a threadbare hunt to open the 5th dungeon by completing the previous 4, the characters barely exist outside of mechanical functions, and since the dungeon follows a roguelike pattern there's no real exploration to be had (doubly so with how small the town is). I can not think of anything worth engaging with in this entire game that isn't a shop or dungeon, and those are uninteresting or frustrating depending on which you're talking about.

I will admit, I didn't beat the whole game. I got through two of the dungeons before deciding that I've had enough, and if you do pick up this game then I really hope you enjoy it more than I did. But I don't see a reason to keep playing this game when the moment to moment gameplay doesn't interest me and there's nothing further ahead worth looking forward to.

Overall, I thoroughly enjoyed this game. I would recommend it to anyone who likes games like Bastion and Stardew Valley. However, I cannot recommend it for the general public in its current state. This game is billed as half store management sim and half rogue-like dungeon crawler. However, I think it's more accurate to describe this game as half of a store management sim combined with half of a rogue-like dungeon crawler. Both of these components lack any kind of depth or nuance. On the store management side of things, all you do is manage your stock, set prices, and upgrade your store. That's it. There's no interaction with the customers. There's no real market fluxation to speak of (other than the popularity of an item declining if it's priced too high, but they still buy the item). There's no competition from other vendors. People come in, buy whatever it is you have, and leave. That's it. On the dungeon crawling side, all you do is kill, loot, and upgrade your equipment. There's no character development. No kind of skills to learn. No real dynamism to combat or the dungeons. You come, you kill, you loot, you leave. That said, even though I feel that this game is actually two halves of two different games, there is something extremely intoxicating about the combination. The games cycle is immensely gratifying that keeps you slavishly hooked. While it lasts, that is. There's a single reason that I cannot recommend this game: There is zero replayability for its length. Every playthrough will have the same 4 dungeons. You'll have the same droll customers. You'll fight off the same theieves. Unlock the same shop upgrades in the same order. Unlock the same town vendors. Upgrade the same equipment. Loot the same items. Fight the same enemies. Sell them for the same prices. Make the same choices. There's zero randomness. Zero incentive to start a new playthrough or to keep playing once it's beat. In my opinion, there's zero reason to start a new game, other than to try to best your previous time, accumulate more wealth, or try to 100% it. My final thoughts are this: The developers of this game have built a game with an amazing foundation. And that shows by this game's immediate success. However, if the developers want this success to continue past the initial release, they're going to have to inject some kind of dynamism into this game ASAP.

The UI could use some polish.

[*] Moving items between inventory and chest is tedious; a mouse would have made a world of difference.
[*] There's no way to tell how many of an item is already owned while in a dungeon.

This game is gorgeous, but very shallow. The cycle: go to the dungeon, get loot. Return from the dungeon, decide which loot to use to upgrade your equipment. Sell the rest. There is no variation. 

The dungeons are very good looking. But they all folow the same formula by design: Three floors ending in a boss. The rooms are randomly generated to a point; the game will tell you how to tell if you're heading toward the next floor.  There are very few hidden secrets/rooms. There are no modifiers like Isaac's curse of the lost or XL floors. There is an interesting mechanic with loot where certain items are "cursed" and will destroy other items or break easily based on where they are placed in your bag. Figuring out how to get the most valuable items home in the biggest quantity while working with the curses is pretty fun and can get exciting when you find something that will turn your trash into a stack of expensive books. 

The combat is decent. You will have to learn what each new enemy does and how to best approach it. There are a variety of weapons, but each is pretty much as good as the last. Find a pair that you like and upgrade them. Once you are able to upgrade your gear, you can trivialize combat pretty easily. There are no special moves, though there are status ailments. I haven't played around with them as usually the best tactic is to hit things in the face until they die. 

The shop is extremely shallow. You set a price for an item and find a "Sweet spot" that customers will buy at. Certain customers prefer certain items, but will buy pretty much anything. There is a demand system where certain items can become more or less popular, letting you adjust prices accordingly, but the customers will always buy at a specific price regardless of demand. The most interesting thing that will happen in your shop is that, occasionally, a thief will try to steal things from you. This person will announce their intent to steal something when they enter the shop and are not difficult to catch. That's it. It is only similar to recettear in that there is a shop and you get the items from a dungeon. No haggling, no relationship with the customers, no crafting. You can eventually decorate your store to add perks like fewer thieves and being able to stay open later, but there's little point to anything other than the items that make the customers tip more. 

Only a select few items are used for gear upgrades. The rest have no use other than to be sold. Value varies wildly between items, and each dungeon has progressively more expensive items. So unless you're upgrading a weapon that you rarely use, there is no reason to backtrack through a dungeon. And, once you can consistently get to the third floor of a dungeon, there's pretty much no use selling the items you can get from earlier floors, as the expensive stuff falls from the sky.

Once you have finished the first dungeon, you have seen all this game has to offer. The cycle continues throughout the rest of the game. There is practically no story to speak of, and the only real motivation is profit, though I've never felt starved for money in the least. If one were to  remove the shop from the game, the dungeons are still formulaic and nothing mind-blowing, and if the dungeon were removed, the shop management is barely a mini-game.

I had a lot of fun with Moonlighter for quite some time. There's a pretty great reward loop, and while it eventually gets old, it's fun to ransack dungeons and outfit your shop for a while. My biggest problem was that it just kind of sputtered out at the end. The final dungeon, if you can call it that, was a letdown, and I never truly felt rewarded for diligently running and upgrading my shop. Still, Moonlighter was a great diversion which I enjoyed. I have high hopes for the sequel and I am looking forward to playing it.

A young merchant yearns to explore the mysteries of the dungeons and become a hero, all while managing his shop and helping his hometown thrive once again, since it’s starting to become a ghost town. Will the hero succeed? Should you bother with this adventure? Well, here’s my take on Moonlighter.


[h1]The Good[/h1][i]Shop Upgrades expands on it’s overall usage.[/i]

When you start using the shop, the first few times, you’ll notice that it functions in a basic manner and are limited on how many items you call sell at a time. Once you start upgrading the shop itself, not only will you be able to sell more items, but you’ll be able to start taking in requests from customers, asking for either a specific item or defeat certain monsters for notes.

You’ll also have a hired assistant sell your items for you while you go through the dungeons and decorate the shop to give you some extra bonuses at the end of the work day. Of course, as you upgrade, you’ll start to have thieves enter your shop, so you’ll have them to keep a watch for, and all this is not counting the other purchases you can make to upgrade the village or the smaller things in your shop.


[h1]The Bad[/h1][i]Bummer Calendar doesn’t keep track of your progress.[/i]

In your Inventory/Journal, you’ll have a section that is your Calendar. This is used to keep track of all the requests that you have taken from the customers in the shop and when they are due… and that’s it.

Now, not having one doesn’t make the game any difficult or anything like that, but once you start taking on requests, the Bestiary could help the player in finding out if monsters drop such items or not.

Moonlighter was funded on Kickstarter and developed by Digital Sun Games based in Valencia, Spain. It combines 2D top-down dungeon crawling with mechanics of management and trading games when selling your loot in your shop.

First of all, Moonlighter is a beautiful game. Detailed and varied pixel art, elaborate animations and atmospheric soundtrack. This is easily the strongest point of the game. The writing and world building on the other hand sticks mostly to explaining the existence of your small town in the proximity of these shifting dungeons. This is basically a reflection of Moonlighter's gameplay, which is somewhat on the weaker side.

But let's start with the most fun part of the gameplay. Moonlighter features a neat twist on managing your inventory while inside the dungeon. Chests may contain enchanted items, which affect loot in adjacent inventory slots. Effects include destroying, disenchanting or instantly teleporting the affected item back to your shop. Combined with limited backpack space in relation to the flood of loot you will acquire in a dungeon, this makes for interesting and difficult decisions while organizing your backpack.

Then again, several others of Moonlighters design decisions simply don't match up. The fun loot system would benefit greatly from having mouse functionality, yet the team deliberately decided to exclude that in favor of "precision controls". But collision detection and animation timings are very inconsistent and the visuals fail to communicate hitboxes as well as damage or invincibility frames. The player's attack angles are limited to the four main directions, yet the game doesn't do much with it. Looking at the dungeons the inspiration by Zelda is obvious. But while Zelda's dungeons are themselves carefully designed puzzles, this apparently doesn't work with procedurally generated content.

Combat is mostly okay, although most attacks being limited to a few directions leads into some balancing issues. This leaves your arsenal with two vastly superior weapons. The big sword allows dealing heavy damage in an area, including diagonally while the bow safely dispatches almost everything which can't attack you at range in a straight line. While enemy types are actually rather varied, I had no problem whatsoever with later enemies, since while their damage ramps up pretty heavily, all their attack patterns are easily exploitable using only these two weapons.

Apart from very few exceptions, progression in Moonlighter is based on stats. Each tier of armor, weapon or healing potion is unlocked with loot from one of the four dungeons, nothing remotely exciting here. You kill the boss of one dungeon, move on to the next one, get the loot from there and upgrade your gear. Loot gets progressively more valuable and many an items' only use is selling them. Armor grants more hitpoints and comes in three flavors which trade defensive stats for movement speed. Weapons can be upgraded on two paths, either granting higher damage or one of four bog-standard status effects: Stun, poison, burn and shock. Weapons and armor can be enchanted to, guess what, raise their stats. Your shop can also be upgraded as a whole or with several items like chests and decorations increasing storage space and the value of sold items. It is worth to mention that you unlock two tools in the first dungeon: One is a mirror which directly sells items for a fraction of their value, the other is a pretty expensive portal which allows re-entering the dungeon at the same spot after visiting the town. And that's pretty much it, basically the whole progression system of Moonlighter is in this single paragraph.

Moonlighter tries to mix several mechanics, yet fails to elaborate on any of them. ARPG combat, procedural dungeon crawling, inventory-management, crafting and town-building all feel shallow. Not a single one of the mechanics feels engaging and challenging on its own and only come together in the amount of gold in your wallet. There are so many different loot items in this game, yet their use is brutally limited. Shop upgrades and decorations are bought from gold only, why don't these upgrades require some loot or another? Why is progression between dungeons and equipment tiers so linear? Giving the player access to the other dungeons earlier and mixing up the required materials for upgrades would undoubtedly increase the feeling I'm challenged to make decisions and plan which item I want to upgrade next. I also would have loved to see the backpack system expanded on. There are tons of effects you could come up with and far too few items have an effect at all. In general, give loot more uses. Far too many items are only there in order to sell them. Finding all those golem blueprints and then not having the ability to craft your own shop assistant was just so horribly disappointing!

In conclusion, is Moonlighter worth your 20 bucks? I would love to say yes, because the mix of dungeon crawling and shopkeeping and crafting definitely sounds pretty intriguing. But the final implementation of each system leaves much to be desired, so until Moonlighter gets several updates or is on a deep sale you should bless somebody else with your money.

I was apprehensive to try Moonlighter at first because I'm not a fan of management simulators, and I was afraid the dungeons would be too difficult to me, but it very quickly became my comfort game and a current favorite! 

While it's by no means the most difficult game out there, you can still get your ass handed to you when you unlock a new level or enter a new dungeon and barge in headfirst, full of hubris. 
The basic premise is rather simple, but the game manages to go about its own mystery in a charming and compelling way. As you make your way through the dungeons, you learn bits and pieces of lore through discovered notes of fallen or missing adventurers, or historic writings left by now (presumably) extinct cultures. All the breadcrumbs lead towards the final, fifth dungeon, without spelling out what you might find there.

The management mechanics are, in my opinion, pretty lightweight and unique. The permantnly restricted inventory slot when you're out adventuring poses an interesting challenge for players, forcing them to strategize and choose which items to keep. This is further compounded as items become more frequently "cursed" as you advance through the dungeon, which affects how you can arrange and carry them. However, while they're called curses, some of them are actually helpful and can mitigate or completely remove the hamful effects of others! There are a few other fun mechanics that allow the player to turn items into gold to free up inventory space, open a portal in a chosen spot, or transport back to town and out of danger in exchange for money. With some caution, the player can easily avoid being defeated and losing their items.

What I found interesting about managing Will's shop Moonlighter was that the player only really gets basic guidelines for the prices, and the rest is up to them to figure out based on customers' reactions and experience. It was a little confusing at first, but it's easy to catch on and figure out approximate values. Similarly, its calendar, merchant's notebook and wishlist system was a little confusing at first, but ultimately easy to understand and very helpful for keeping track of items and quests. There is no micomanagement in the game and the crafting system isn't super expansive either, so those who enjoy the grind of those aspects might find themselves disappointed. For me this was a plus because it keeps things more fast paced and less overwhelming, while still allowing enough creativity and fun with its established lore & mechanics.

Moonlighter is, of course, repetitive/cyclical as every game in its genre, but it still manages to remain fresh in its gameplay and charming in its mystery. If you're looking for a game that will make you grind endlessly, make you read every item to understand the lore, or portray indepth emotional struggles, this game isn't for you. But if you'd prefer something more casual and fun that still manages to pack a punch, stylistically beautiful and unique in the way it connects its lore and gameplay, then I'd warmly recommend you give Moonlighter a shot. :)

I've yearned for another mercantile game similar to Recettear for years. I rooted for this game from when it was first revealed as it looked like it could be the one. However upon playing it, that's sadly not the case.

 - Selling items in your shop is disappointingly simplistic. Gauge out what an item's value is and then always sell it at that price.
 - The lack of any time limitations in the game (ex. paying off a loan) means that there is no pressure to maximize your profits. One will simply return to the dungeon each night and sell the spoils each day until enough gold is obtained to buy whatever upgrades they want. This essentially turns the shopkeeping section of the game into a slow way to "sell all" of your unwanted items.
 - The combat is sufficient and fairly standard, common in most roguelikes. Nothing special or super deep, but I believe that is for the best in a mercantile genre game; the role of the dungeon delving should be to acquire valuable treasures, not slay the mightiest foes. However, because the mercantile section of the game is lacking, it really leaves the combat to hold the game up on its own, which it struggles to do.

Moonlighter is a beautiful looking game that suffers from an under-designed economy. I think with more fleshing out of options/systems/complexity for running a business, the game could truly be a superb shopkeeping game.

I just want to preface the rest of this by saying I made the mistake of watching a few videos on youtube about how to finish the final boss. My advice: don't do it. Just read this. As of late I seem to run into the same problem where I find the game either about right or even kinda easy and then the final boss is so ludicrously difficult that I eventually give up, give it a negative review and move on with my life - the equivalent of having a hissy, then taking my bat and ball and going home. Other people here in the reviews complained about the combat being jank but I only felt that before I did any upgrades. Once he got good enough to control, each dungeon was only brickwalled off because of a lack of upgrade. The grind doesn't [i]feel[/i] too bad but the hours go by super quick when dungeon 4 doesn't give you as many items as the 3 previous dungeons. The people in these reviews who said they were getting so much money by the end of it, is only somewhat true. You DO make a lot of money. I would just put down a portal back to camp when my bag got too full or I was running out of life and I could come back to the spot in the dungeon.

Another game I'm very mixed on.  I almost gave this a thumbs-down at the end because I was a bit over it all and was thinking "this needs to end soon", which isn't great for a game.  Thankfully it did end, and the ending was ok, so ... there you go.

I did really enjoy the early stages of this.  The music is great, the art is great.  Little things like the head silhouettes for 'yes' and 'no' just pleased me greatly for some reason.  The hybrid game worked well at the beginning - dungeon crawling at night and then running the shop by day.  It's simple, but surprisingly rewarding ... for a while.

Hybrid games are challenging to balance over the playtime though, and so it is here.  The shop aspect kind of fell away in terms of importance and enjoyability.  Perversely (in my opinion) the upgrades to the shop make the experience less enjoyable, more of a chore, and I would argue the final upgrade of the base game shop is basically a downgrade on-balance.  Being clearer about what the upgrades mean, or tying the challenges of the shop to some other aspect of progression (like dungeons cleared or something) would have been nice, and then the upgrades would feel more like rewards leading to solving problems rather than creating new problems.

The identification of price points is a cute idea (for a shop game) but the actual mechanics were a bit frustrating.  I think a bit more thought and creativity here would not have gone astray.

The dungeon crawling is ok.  I would have liked the experience to be a bit richer, but it's ok.  For a while.

The story is kind of neat - it's not really a game that needs the story, but the story that is there is intriguing.

So yeah, I think I'm done with the game now without playing NG+ or the DLC.  But it is enjoyable for a while, and for that reason I think it's worth checking out.

Quite nice dungeoncrawling, but pretty short and overly simplistic; shop keeping seems like a total afterthought. 

The game initially plays quite nice and is a pretty good ARPG dungeoncrawling experience. The movement and controls are (apart from some minor hitbox issues) fine and responsive. 

The fighting mechanics (and that's more or less all that is to dungeoncrawling in this game) are very simplistic. 
Every weapon has an normal and a charge attack. That's it. No special attacks, no combos, nothing. 
This coupled with the relative repetitiveness of the dungeons (while there are 4 stylistically different dungeons, with different enemies, enemy variety within a given dungeon isn't particularly great) will probably lead quite a few people to feel bored with the experience, after some time playing, despite the overall game being relatively (roughly 10-15 hrs) short. 
Apart from perhaps achievement collecting, there also isn't any kind of post end content. 
Despite the dungeons being randomized, they are almost (a few hidden and side areas exist) completely linear, with fixed bosses at the end of every dungeon and a linear crafting/progression system, so replayability isn't great either. 

Instead of a traditional leveling system, Moonlighter uses a (again) pretty simple crafting system. 
Each of the five weapons/styles (sword&shield, greatsword, spear, claws and bows) has two linear upgrade paths, one with more alpha damage, one with less but a dot effect.
Similarly the three armor slots (head, body and feet) have options that give low defense and speed, medum defense or high defense at the price of a speed penalty.
Nothing too fancy or complicated but also not too bad, this serves ok-ish as the games primary (despite this major upgrades, there are also smaller and cheaper minor upgrades to specific weapons) progression system. 

What is really bad though are the shop mechanics. While the game is supposedly centered around you managing an item shop (though to be more precise in this game you sell mostly materials; so a materials shop?), the underlying system is so simplistic, that it completely feels like an afterthought, and at times one might even wonder, why it was ever implemented this way (instead of in example simply selling the items to merchants like is common in other [A]RPGS).

The system boils down to gauging what price you can get for an item (initially a pretty random exercise, as you are only told the maximum and minimum price of items in a rather long list; fortunately feedback on the item price is saved), setting that price and waiting until someone buys said item...

While there are supposedly other mechanics at work (like demand up and down), their influence on the game seems to be extremely miniscule (I never understood, what they're supposed to do). 
They surely don't affect the price people are buying items for in any way. If I actually had to hazard a guess, I’d say that these supposed "mechanics" aren't implemented at all. 
The shop can also be upgraded with so called decorations, but apart from sale price raising ones the effect of the other ones are pretty minimal and not really worth mentioning. 

Later on you may also take requests for specific items, but by the time you have unlocked this option, you will be able to sell items at a higher price, than what you get for fulfilling these requests, so this is also completely pointless.

All in all the shop management is so simple and feels almost completely pointless, one can not but wonder, why it exists in this form in the game at all. 

Unfortunately, while the dungeoncrawling mechanics itself aren't bad, they are in my opinion not diverse and varied enough, that they could carry the game on their own. 

If someone is interested in the premise of running an item shop in a fantasy world I’d semi-recommend Recettear: An Item Shop's Tale instead, though that game is not without its fair share of issues (mainly the dungeoneering actually being pretty bad and a somewhat… controversial progression system) either.

As it does not I have chosen to not recommend this game, because while the game isn't really terrible or even bad, there is also simply no one i could in good conscience recommend the game for... especially not at full price.

Moonlighter looks great and has a solid, distinct art style. Moonlighter has great music and sound effects. Moonlighter has a good concept. The cursed items impact on inventory management is interesting. The end dungeon bosses are well constructed.

That's where my praise ends. You have unlocked the entire game after the tutorial ends. When you've sold some items and gone through a dungeon, you've experienced everything there is. The gameplay loop is that simple. You will be grinding for a while for every upgrade, fighting the exact same monsters in the exact same environment. The keyboard controls are abysmal, to the point where it's almost unplayable. Nothing on the store page suggests that you need a controller to play. With that said, the gamepad controls aren't much better. The game also does not fully support the dualshock 4, instead having every button prompt displaying xbox controls. After trying one dungeon with a gamepad, I went back to my keyboard. Not keyboard and mouse, just keyboard, as the mouse has nothing bound to it in the game. You can rebind the controls if you want, but by god is the default just abysmal. It's hard to imagine whomever set the defaults ever played with them.

Combat isn't great, mostly because of how poor the hitboxes are. If you are too close to something, you are unable to damage it. The shield block window does not line up with the animation. The roll i frame window is incredibly small and feels inconsistent. Flying enemies do damage at the start of their animation window (which is also the time they are vulnerable), leaving you with little choice but to take some damage to kill them. Of the five weapon options, gloves and sword+shield have too little range to be very useful, the heavy swords are too slow and clumsy to deal with many enemies, and the bow is okay. The spear is just by far the best.

The town superficially grows and reacts to your progress. You can spend money to upgrade things and open new shops, but it feels like a checklist rather than a town growing. None of the dialogue sells you on the former bustling town returning to its glory days that the game wants you to believe. The one interesting character you can talk to is out of the way and only rarely gets new dialogue options. This is a stark contrast to Recettear, where the dialogue is engaging and the character development feels genuine.

The biggest issue I have with Moonlighter is how buggy it is. About once every half hour I get a nice exception notification that tells me Moonlighter needs to close. Since the game also runs on a very similar save system to Stardew Valley, where it only saves your progress when you sleep for the day, crashing in the middle of a day just feels awful. That's actually why I'm writing this review: Moonlighter crashed while I was heading back to sleep and I lost a days worth of progress.

If you played Recettear and want more, or you were turned off by Recettear's art style, buy this on sale and give it a shot. The shallow mechanics and overall unpolished nature make me not willing to recommend it at $20. Perhaps I'll change my mind as I play it more, but I'm not optimistic.

Great game overall. Fun dungeon crawler with rogue-lite (I hope I spelled that right) elements, with nice, responsive fighting system that emphasizes evasion over tanking damage. The game offers a number of weapons, each with their own fighting style. There is some variety of monsters with different attack patters, and a number of boss fights. There is a "new game plus" mode that makes the game a bit longer and a bit harder.

Difficulty is variable, personally I enjoyed it the most on "easy" difficulty, although "normal" wasn't THAT hard (just a bit too hard for me personally).

There's also a shop-keeper... mini-game? Which is also fun and allows you to change pace for a little while.

Music is nice, not transistor-nice, not bastion-nice, but generally pleasant and not annoying.
Graphics are well drawn, even though pretty simplistic.

The DLC is also fun, giving you an endless dungeon (not exactly endless but indefinitely replayable). Some achievements are pretty difficult, but it is all do-able (sadly, some take MANY tries if you're not very good with a controller, I, for one, am not).

Personally, I'd prefer several stages for each boss fight when either boss attack pattern or game arena (or both) change to some extent, extending the fight and adding variety.

Hoping to see a new game by this developer some time in the future.

Moonlighter is an intriguing game that melds popular mechanics, combat, crafting, objectives, as well as the desire of many to try the life an adventurer from the other side of the counter. While the game isn’t perfect, it has charm to spare. I will be reviewing the game in some depth so please beware of spoilers ahead. Here are some notes on certain aspects of the game:

  !Spoilers! !Spoilers! !Spoilers! !Spoilers! !Spoilers! !Spoilers! !Spoilers! !Spoilers! !Spoilers! !Spoilers! !Spoilers! !Spoilers!

Design/Core Gameplay Loop: This game begins by offering your first short-term goals, tackling your first dungeon and beginning the process of bringing your shop back to prosperity, and your long-term goal of opening the fifth door or the final dungeon. The player accomplishes this by combating his way through the dungeons in a linear approach while simultaneously selling goods he has found in the dungeons to buy better gear. The combat, while originally fun to develop and practice, is very quickly mastered. More on this later. The mercantile aspect of the game too is something that could have been done differently. While it’s originally fun to bring back goods to sell in the store, you very quickly realize that your only selling goods to upgrade your armor and weapons so that you can head back into the dungeon. At one point, I left the store alone for nearly an in-game week and no grievances were issued and there are no risks for doing so. As a package, Moonlighter looks fun from the outside but once you begin to play, you will quickly notice that it’s a very shallow experience. 

Combat: There is little to no depth in the combat system that Moonlighter employs. Once you have gone through the first dungeon, you know nearly all the ways the enemy AI will behave. While I believe that this was an attempt to employ a novice/proficient/mastery flow in combat, I think it falls flat due to the lack of additional enemy behaviors as the game goes on. The only thing that changes is enemy looks, health, and damage output. However, the enemy bosses, or guardians in this case, are a reprieve from the monotone combat by bringing in new combat procedures. Unfortunately, this too falls short as many of the guardians can be defeated easily using the spear or the bow. I found that if I stood in a particular spot in the first guardian fight, I could kill the guardian without being targeted. The third boss was probably the most developed fight as it required the player to use multiple weapons and employ the dodge mechanic in order to succeed in defeating it. The game tries to increase flow through more enemies and more difficult fights but it tries to implement this through the usual more health and damage that is found in many games that aren’t fully developed. It seems like the combat was into the end product and it shows. 

Weapons/Armor/Items: In RPG’s, a player expects to have the options to use many types of weapons or at least multiple variants to a single weapon. Moonlighter gives you five weapons that you can choose from and two weapon trees that can be invested in. The first is raw weapon damage and the second is an elemental attribute to the weapon with less damage output. This is an interesting option to have but you can only build a weapon with an elemental attribute once you go to the dungeon where enemies use that elemental attribute. The elemental weapons do cause some DPS but this is a fast paced game where enemies can easily damage you if you leave them unattended. Thus, the weapons with more damage output are just more viable choices. The armor is a weird choice for a game that is supposed to be all about staying on the move in combat and mastering the dodge mechanic. The armor comes in three tiers. The first tier is lighter and allows for faster movement but offers inferior protection to the second tier. The second tier has zero debufs and buffs but offers better protection than the first tier. This is where the design choice for the armor is odd. The second tier doesn’t slow down the player and the player can still keep up with enemies fine as long as he has played the game and learned from the dungeons. The enemies are tailored to this and perform fairly consistently across the board in terms of speed and complexity. The third tier of armor is heavier and slows down the player. While this seems to make sense as the player is trading protection for speed, the game seems to be tailored to a certain speed that the player can obtain by staying in the second tier of armor or the first. The third tier that offers the most protection also makes the game the most difficult by impeding the very basis on which the mechanics are founded. The saving grace of the items are the potions and enchantments. The potions are rarely drops in the dungeons and you never have enough if you play risky and get hurt. You also can’t place more potions in your hot bar as long as there are enemies in the room. This creates risk and accentuates player flow. The enchantments too are difficult to obtain as the player needs to make the conscious choice to leave behind other goods for the store and to take the necessary goods to enchant a weapon. This aspect of the game was well thought out and balanced. 

Bugs/Optimizations: There are a few bugs in Moonlighter but the ones that you encounter destroy the flow of the game. Theses bugs include guardians not being able to hurt you, the inventory bugging out and the player not able to sell something from it and being unable to teleport home at times. The choice of whether this is playable is up to you, but I found it very difficult to look past. The game is very optimized, and I had no problems with performance. 
Ambience: The art and audio in Moonlighter are very likely the highest points in the game. It is very pretty and even with all of the issues that I had with the game, I found myself wanting to keep playing the game. Even moments that I was bored standing the in the store waiting for the money to buy a potion, I was kept occupied listening to the soundtrack and the varying NPC’s. 

Conclusion: I found that I wanted to complete the game regardless of the problems that I found. The animations and ambience are top notch. However, the combat is very shallow, the mercantile aspect of the game seems like a skin over the usual collect and sell drops, and the game is very short. Although I enjoyed playing the game, I can’t recommend it with all the problems that I discovered and the shallow approach to design.

Really enjoyed this game! It's a fun hack-and-slash rogue-type game. 

Pro: the game is easy to look at the UI and the sound design and music are really nice in the game. The fact that it's a pixelated game gives it an old-timey feeling but with a new modern spin to it, 

Con: playing the game with a controller is a MUST for this game... I have tried playing it with a mouse and keyboard, but the character doesn't roll well... Although at times even with the controller the character doesn't turn the best either, which can be annoying when trying to void enemy hits. 

But I would recommend this game for those who enjoy rogue-like games. Plus I really enjoy the music and the art style of the game.

The game sounds and looks amazing, the gameplay is very repetetive and unrewarding though. You enter a Dungeon with three stages and need to fight your way through with a Boss at the end of the last stage. The Dungeons themself are randomly generated, but you will basically have seen everything after your first or second try. You collect loot to bring to your own shop, where you have to "find out" the prices of the items and sell them to get money so you can upgrade your gear. Sounds cool, but the shopkeeping at this point is just standing around, waiting for NPC to come in, pressing a button after they selected an item and then replacing that item with another one. The upgrade system in this game is even worse. There are three armor sets, but all the upgrades of the different sets look exactly the same. You can choose between a few different weapons and the weapon upgrades actually look different, but the special attacks and the general gameplay doesnt change. at all. If you want to improve your weapon you just get some random crystals you get spammed with in every dungeon and money from the repetetive shopkeeping and throw it at an NPC to get more damage so you can repeat the same thing in the next dungeon and then the dungeon after it. 
I really like the idea behind this game, but it definitely needs some work. I would love to play this with more customisation, a more complex shop system and more gameplay variety like different upgrades to weapons and maybe a skilltree.

- Can get the same gameplay in Recettear, Hyperlight Drifter, Binding of Isaac
- Town is bland, story is boring

If you're thinking of buying this because reviews are telling you things like "It's like Stardew Valley", don't. Wait for updates or a sale.

Also, personal gripe, pre-order contrent that you can't get anymore.

It takes a while to get use to the mechanics, despite the tutorial being decent. However, the learning curve so far is fairly quick to get to a level where you are confident enough to learn the rest at your own pace.

As for the game itself, and that is coming from a one hour in review, you loot random dungeons (of increasing difficulties if you so choose) and sell the most valuable loot/artifacts in your shop. There seems to be a crafting system once you start improving the town so cheaper more common mats will probably be used there (along with possible rarer ones). The selling price is set by the player and based on the feedback of the customers or potential customers, you adjust it until you find the best price. A supply/demand system is supposed to be built-in as well but I'm to early on to comment on that.

Overall fun game, kind of if Zelda had crossed with Diablo (proceduraly generated dungeons) and a shopkeeping game.
There is literally no mouse support... extremely annoying to play if you use keyboard instead of a controller. Especially the menus. Feels like a cheap console port to PC.

Personally, after spending 15h in this game I do not recommend it. It's totally average! 
If you like rogue-like games, play Binding of Isaac, Hades, whatever, it will be better. If you like shop management/economy games, choose every other game of this genre, it will be better... After playing 1h you know everything, you saw everything, there won't be anything else, but a ton of grinding. 
- Controls are irritating, especially during shop gameplay. 
- Story is... what story?
- Music - random elevator music, nothing memorable.
- Visuals are nice. Good looking pixel art.

The game is addicting for a couple of hours but sadly, it can't keep up to that expectation for the entire playthrough. It gets monotonous and formulaic after a while and you might as well as not finish the game since it's the same as beating the first level.

I got pretty annoyed because I was hyped about the art, the concept... everything!

Great little game. It was a lot shorter than I expected it to be (my first playthrough finished at about 9 hours and 30 minutes), but I thoroughly enjoyed it.

My main disappointment is the "roguelike" aspect. I expected some of the character progression systems being tied to procedural generation (random stats on weapons, permanent player upgrades found in the dungeon, etc), but it's actually very linear.
